responses.strategic_rationale: The plan centers on establishing a physical residential research unit in Bonn to study adult NREM parasomnias with rigorous, technology-supported data capture in a controlled yet domestic environment. Core tensions arise from balancing high-fidelity physiological data collection with participant comfort, privacy, safety, and sustainable funding, while delivering timely methods validation and longitudinal phenotyping. Scaling capacity, governing data access, refining automated triage, and strengthening staffing without compromising ethics or data integrity are the primary levers that will determine whether this early-stage facility can prove a robust, generalizable blueprint for future interventions and multi-site expansion.

levers.name: Residential capture model scale
levers.consequences: Expanding the residential capture model increases participant throughput and data yield, accelerating method validation and longitudinal phenotyping. The trade-off is higher capital and staffing demands, and potential strain on quality controls if onboarding and training do not scale in parallel.
options: Expand to a 12-suite footprint only after predefined data-quality milestones are met and staffing ratios validated in a dry-run, ensuring operational resilience before scaling.
Optimize eight-suite operations with a modular room reconfiguration plan that can add two additional suites within six weeks if early data show stable throughput.
Maintain eight suites and implement a rigorous process-review to prioritize workflow efficiency, recruitment criteria tightening, and enhanced event-triage accuracy before any expansion.
levers.review_lever: Expansion creates greater throughput but increases capital and staffing pressures; the options do not address long-term sustainability of quality controls and staff fatigue under sustained growth.

levers.name: Data governance and privacy framing
levers.consequences: Pulling this lever reshapes access, sharing, and auditing of data, strengthening privacy and compliance. The downstream implication is slower collaboration and longer turnarounds for external validation while governance processes mature.
options: Adopt a strict de-identification protocol and access controls to align with privacy constraints, enabling broader, safer data sharing while risking reduced granularity for researchers.
Establish a tiered data access framework with researcher-reviewed requests and data-use agreements, balancing openness with participant privacy and practical data-anonymization challenges.
Pilot on-site data governance with automated auditing and consent-tracking to ensure compliance, while implementing governance delays that may slow data release and collaboration.
levers.review_lever: Privacy protections slow data sharing and complicate multi-site collaboration, and the three options do not resolve how to harmonize anonymization standards across collaborators or how to audit data provenance efficiently.

levers.name: Semi-automated event-triage tooling
levers.consequences: Implementing semi-automated triage improves reliability of event labeling and reduces manual review workload. A potential downside is slower adaptation to new or rare patterns if systems rely on established rules or require extensive retraining.
options: Develop a rule-based event-triage pipeline that flags likely parasomnia events and routes to dual human scoring, prioritizing transparency and reproducibility over raw speed.
Implement a learning-enhanced triage module trained on annotated data with regular recalibration, prioritizing accuracy but requiring larger data sets and extended validation.
Leverage ensemble scoring combining sensor streams with clinical metadata to reduce false positives while preserving interpretability for clinicians.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off centers on accuracy gains versus adaptability; the options do not specify how models will remain robust to shifting data distributions and new event morphologies across participants.

levers.name: Night-shift staffing and safety margin
levers.consequences: Pulling this lever rebalances coverage to maintain safety and data integrity during high-activity periods, but increases training, fatigue risk, and administrative overhead if shifts rotate too rapidly.
options: Adopt a rotating night-shift model with cross-trained technicians to maintain coverage while reducing fatigue, improving safety but increasing training overhead.
Contract external on-call technicians for peak nights to bolster response capacity during high-event windows, reducing staffing burden during low-rate periods.
Invest in a dedicated night-shift coordinator and protocol-driven handover rituals to improve incident response while raising administrative coordination complexity.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off between safety coverage and training/coordination overhead; the options do not specify how fatigue will be systematically managed across extended pilot.

levers.name: Recruitment and inclusion strategy
levers.consequences: Pulling this lever broadens the pool of eligible participants and improves representativeness, but can introduce greater heterogeneity in episode patterns and increase screening burdens.
options: Expand recruitment to national networks and international collaborators to diversify sample, potentially extending recruitment timelines but improving generalizability.
Standardize pre-admission tele-screening to quickly assess eligibility, reducing in-person burden while potentially excluding nuanced cases.
Forge formal referral agreements with regional clinics and train staff to collect standardized collateral histories, improving yield from referrals while demanding closer coordination.
levers.review_lever: Expansion improves representativeness but risks longer recruitment pipelines; the options do not address the balance between strict inclusion criteria and practical enrollment speed.

levers.name: Tiered sensing modalities and monitoring cadence
levers.consequences: Tiered sensing increases data richness by layering low-burden nightly monitoring with scheduled enhanced nights, while preserving participant comfort. The trade-off is added maintenance, calibration, and scheduling complexity.
options: Maintain nightly low-burden monitoring with dry-electrode EEG headbands and mattress sensors, ensuring participant comfort and high retention.
Schedule enhanced nights with fuller PSG montage on specific nights to capture diagnostic detail while preserving routine sleep burden for most nights.
Implement escalation nights triggered by technician flags to capture recurrence at clinical-grade resolution, balancing data richness with scheduling flexibility.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off lies between data richness and participant burden; the options do not specify clear escalation thresholds that prevent overly long stays or participant fatigue.

responses.strategic_rationale: The Bonn residential parasomnia program must balance ecological validity with robust safety, scalable operations, and rigorous data protocols. The six levers below target environment realism, adaptive sensing, phased expansion, adjudication reliability, safety architecture, and data stream prioritization to de-risk scale while preserving data integrity and scientific value.

levers.name: Naturalistic environment fidelity versus safety constraints
levers.consequences: Direct effect: Preserving a domestic ambiance supports natural sleep behavior and participant comfort, boosting ecological validity. Downstream implication: Safety protocols and restricted-opening windows increase intervention latency and staff workload, trading off rapid emergency responsiveness for data realism.
options: Maintain a home-like suite layout while deploying automated fall-detection and real-time alert systems to enable rapid intervention when needed.
Implement a modular safety protocol that can temporarily upgrade to clinical fixtures on high-risk nights to preserve data quality without constant clinicalization.
Adopt a staged ambiance strategy with routine safety drills and increased staff presence during observations to balance ecological validity with reliable emergencies.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: realism may erode rapid intervention capabilities; gap: none of the options specify exact staffing or budget thresholds required to maintain safety without compromising ecological validity.

levers.name: Adaptive sensing tier allocation
levers.consequences: Direct effect: tailoring sensing intensity reduces participant burden and data load, improving study compliance and processing efficiency. Downstream implication: increased complexity of data integration and potential gaps if thresholds are mis-specified or misapplied across participants.
options: Implement real-time sensor allocation that ramps up data capture only when live indicators suggest risk of events.
Run scheduled calibration windows to reallocate sensors based on annotation throughput and storage limits.
Adopt a mixed-sensor approach with continuous low-burden streams for all participants while deploying episodic high-fidelity PSG on confirmed events.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: miscalibrated thresholds can miss events or inflate false positives; gap: lacks explicit criteria for threshold setting, validation, and cross-participant consistency.

levers.name: Evidence-driven expansion gating
levers.consequences: Direct effect: expansion proceeds only after predefined data quality and safety KPIs are achieved, reducing premature scaling. Downstream implication: this gating can slow growth and morale if milestones prove hard to reach, potentially affecting funding momentum.
options: Adopt a formal milestone-based expansion plan where additional suites unlock only after predefined data quality and safety KPIs are met.
Accelerate expansion by conducting a parallel pilot in a neighboring facility to validate metrics before Bonn scale-up.
Delay expansion until cost-performance alignment is demonstrated by independent audits and external review.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: growth is gated and may delay impact; gap: lacks explicit thresholds for what constitutes acceptable data quality and safety performance.

levers.name: Human-in-the-loop adjudication workflow redesign
levers.consequences: Direct effect: prioritizes accuracy while reducing backlog by routing uncertain cases to senior raters; downstream implication: increased cognitive load on senior scorers and potential bottlenecks if escalation capacity is insufficient.
options: Institute a tiered review process where junior scorers flag potential events for senior raters, reducing backlog.
Implement randomized double scoring on a subset to estimate inter-rater reliability and adjust training.
Centralize adjudication with time-boxed review windows to ensure timely scoring while preserving accuracy.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: efficiency gains may come at the cost of consistency if senior reviewers are overloaded; gap: no defined target for acceptable inter-rater reliability.

levers.name: Participant safety and emergency response architecture
levers.consequences: Direct effect: formalizes response times and escalation paths, reducing risk during events. Downstream implication: higher staffing requirements and potential rigidity limit scheduling flexibility and data-collection variety.
options: Establish a dedicated on-site emergency response protocol with predefined escalation pathways and staff rotation to minimize response latency.
Develop a risk-based staffing framework that adjusts coverage levels based on participant risk profiles and observed event frequency.
Create a drill schedule and incident logging system that trains staff and documents learning for continuous improvement.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: safety-driven staffing increases fixed costs and may constrain trial flexibility; gap: lacks explicit criteria for triggering staffing adjustments or drill frequency.

levers.name: Prioritization of data streams and archival policy
levers.consequences: Direct effect: defines which streams receive higher fidelity storage and processing, enabling focused analyses. Downstream implication: potential biases in data coverage and reduced availability of lower-priority streams for secondary analyses.
options: Define a data tiering plan that prioritizes high-resolution EEG streams for a subset of nights while maintaining baseline records for all participants.
Implement on-site preprocessing to compress and anonymize data before transfer to university storage, reducing bandwidth needs.
Establish a policy for real-time quality checks and automated metadata tagging to improve later manual scoring efficiency.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off: selective fidelity may bias outcomes if not balanced; gap: lacks criteria for deciding which nights or participants receive higher fidelity data.

responses.strategic_rationale: The plan confronts the core tensions of safety, data quality, participant comfort, staffing feasibility, and regulatory compliance within a residential sleep research unit. The levers focus on escalation discipline, data workflow efficiency, consent governance, environmental design, validation of sensor streams against PSG gold standards, and adaptive consent architectures. Together they aim to deliver robust methods validation and longitudinal phenotyping while guarding against burnout, bias, and misalignment with ethical and governance requirements. This set seeks scalable pathways for phase-two expansions and grant-readiness without compromising safety or scientific integrity.

levers.name: Escalation-night protocol harmonization
levers.consequences: Pulling this lever tightens escalation-night procedures to yield richer event data during clinically flagged nights, while increasing staff fatigue and scheduling overhead across the unit. A downstream implication is that non-escalation nights may face slower response times or reduced protective coverage if staffing becomes stretched, potentially impacting safety margins and study consistency.
options: Institute a tiered escalation-night protocol that triggers full PSG when predefined cues appear, coordinating schedule and staffing accordingly to improve data richness.
Pilot real-time rule-based event tagging to reduce unnecessary escalations while maintaining data integrity and clinician oversight.
Restructure night-shift schedules to concentrate escalation-night duties on peak-event windows, balancing fatigue with consistent data capture reliability.
levers.review_lever: This lever shifts heavy escalation duties onto staff, improving data during events at the cost of fatigue and complex scheduling; the three options leave unaddressed whether automation can sustain scaling without increasing risk.

levers.name: Continuous annotation throughput optimization
levers.consequences: Pulling this lever reduces backlog and speeds results, but may pressure raters to hurry judgments, risking variability without robust calibration. A downstream implication is that timing gains could erode reliability if ongoing training is neglected.
options: Implement a double-scoring workflow with parallel independent raters during high-load periods to accelerate adjudication while preserving reliability.
Standardize real-time annotation templates and keyboard shortcuts to minimize scorer cognitive load and reduce timing variance across nights.
Cross-train technicians and scorers across roles to quickly reallocate tasks during unexpected staff shortages without compromising data quality.
levers.review_lever: The trade-off is potential consistency risk when distributing workload across multiple raters; the three options do not guarantee durable inter-rater reliability under variable study pace.

levers.name: Collateral history integration and consent governance
levers.consequences: Pulling this lever enriches event-context data and strengthens recruitment accuracy, but it risks introducing selection bias if collateral availability unevenly maps to participant demographics. A downstream implication is that data richness could come at the expense of broader representativeness.
options: Integrate bed-partner collateral history interviews into eligibility screening and consent processes to strengthen event-context data and improve inclusion.
Adopt tiered consent stacking allowing participants to authorize broader data use gradually as trust and familiarity build.
Create a blinded collateral-check protocol that ensures collateral data usage is de-emphasized when consent is limited and bias is minimized.
levers.review_lever: The trade-off is richer contextual data versus recruitment bias; the options omit a clear mechanism to ensure representativeness when collateral availability varies.

levers.name: Environmental design for safety without clinical feel

A downstream implication is potential cost pressure and longer setup times for each room, which could constrain scalability.
options: Redesign room layouts to maximize naturalistic behavior while integrating fail-safe features and rapid escape routes clearly marked for safety.
Implement non-intrusive safety monitoring that preserves ambience, such as flexible door alarms and padding, to maintain comfort without compromising detection.
Calibrate acoustic treatment and lighting to minimize arousal without triggering artificial constraints on sleep behavior.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off involves safety margins vs ambient authenticity; none of the options resolve how to uniformly implement room designs across all suites while maintaining safety protocol adherence.

levers.name: Redundant sensor fusion validation against PSG gold standard
levers.consequences: Pulling this lever increases confidence in event mappings by cross-checking streams against PSG benchmarks, improving data interpretation and reliability. A downstream trade-off is higher resource use and longer data processing cycles, which may delay timely insights.
options: Schedule periodic cross-validation sessions where selected nights receive full PSG alongside ongoing in-bed sensors to verify event mappings.
Establish a blinded adjudication subset where certified PSG reviewers compare low-burden streams against full PSG to measure accuracy.
Develop a data reconciliation protocol that flags discordant classifications between sensor streams for joint review and learning.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off is accuracy gain vs resource burden; the options do not specify how to sustain timely analyses if validation cycles lengthen.

levers.name: Adaptive consent architecture for longitudinal stay
levers.consequences: Pulling this lever aligns data-sharing preferences with evolving participant comfort, potentially improving retention and consent accuracy. A downstream implication is regulatory and operational complexity in managing dynamic preferences across multiple streams and timepoints.
options: Offer dynamic consent checkpoints at mid-stay iterations, enabling participants to adjust data-sharing preferences as circumstances evolve.
Pilot opt-in opt-out toggles for specific data streams to empower participant control without disrupting study continuity.
Create feedback loops where consent choices inform future communication strategies and retention incentives to reduce dropout risk.
levers.review_lever: Trade-off is participant autonomy versus governance overhead; the options do not address how to prevent consent drift from weakening data completeness.

system_prompt:
You are an expert strategic analyst. Generate solution space parameters following these directives:

1. **Output Requirements**
   - You must generate 5 to 7 levers per response.
   - Each lever's `options` field must contain exactly 3 qualitative strategic choices as plain strings.

2. **Lever Quality Standards**
   - Consequences: describe the direct effect of pulling this lever, then at least one downstream implication or trade-off in qualitative terms. Exact numbers will be determined further downstream — here the goal is to articulate the cause-effect relationship clearly. Target length: 2–3 sentences.
   - Options MUST:
     • Represent genuinely distinct strategic pathways (not just labels)
     • Include at least one unconventional or non-obvious approach
     • NO prefixes (e.g., "Option A:", "Choice 1:")

3. **Strategic Framing**
   - Name each lever using language drawn directly from the project's own domain — avoid formulaic patterns or repeated prefixes
   - Frame options as complete strategic approaches
   - Ensure levers challenge core project assumptions

4. **Validation Protocols**
   - For `review_lever`:
     A short critical review — identify the primary trade-off this lever introduces, then state the specific gap the three options leave unaddressed.
     Examples:
     - "Switching from seasonal contract labor to year-round employees stabilizes harvest quality, but the idle-wage burden during the 5-month off-season adds a fixed cost that erases the per-unit savings unless utilization reaches year-round levels."
     - "Each additional clinical site requires its own IRB approval, site-initiation visit, and staff credentialing — a sequential overhead that compounds rather than parallelizes, so doubling site count does not halve enrollment time."
     - "Pooling catastrophe risk across three coastal regions reduces expected annual loss on paper, but a single regional hurricane season can correlate all three simultaneously, turning the diversification assumption into a concentration risk at the worst possible moment."
     Do not use square brackets or placeholder text.

5. **Prohibitions**
   - NO prefixes/labels in options (e.g., "Option A:", "Choice 1:")
   - NO generic option labels (e.g., "Optimize X", "Tolerate Y")
   - NO placeholder consequences or bracket-wrapped templates
   - NO specific numbers, percentages, or monetary amounts — describe effects qualitatively
   - NO marketing language (e.g., "game-changing", "cutting-edge", "revolutionary")

6. **Length Limits**
   - Keep each `review_lever` to one sentence (20–40 words). State the trade-off and the gap concisely.
   - Each option should be a concrete, actionable approach (at least 15 words with an action verb) — not a short label or vague aspiration
   - Maintain parallel grammatical structure across options
   - Ensure options are self-contained descriptions
user_prompt:
File 'plan.txt':
Plan:
Establish a 3-year residential longitudinal research unit in Bonn, Germany, for the study of adult NREM parasomnias — sleepwalking, confusional arousals, and sleep terrors — with a secondary exploratory arm for REM sleep behavior disorder under a separate protocol with dedicated neurologic screening, reflecting RBD's distinct clinical trajectory per current AASM guidance. The facility is affiliated with University Hospital Bonn's Department of Epileptology, leveraging its existing long-term video-EEG monitoring culture, and addresses a specific methodological gap: traditional single-night polysomnography rarely captures infrequent parasomnia events, while outpatient actigraphy lacks physiological resolution. The unit houses 8 active sleep suites at launch in a converted residential property in a quiet Bonn neighborhood, renovated for safety (padded corridor edges, restricted-opening windows, silent exterior door alarms, fire safety, acoustic treatment, network cabling, accessibility modifications) while preserving a domestic feel — if the environment is too clinical, naturalistic behavior is suppressed. Physical capacity exists for 12 suites, but expansion is deferred until the pilot proves acceptable data quality, manageable false alarm rates, safe staffing ratios, and usable annotation throughput. Sensing uses a tiered acquisition model: nightly low-burden monitoring via dry-electrode EEG headbands, contact-free mattress sensors, unobtrusively mounted infrared cameras, ambient microphones, and environmental sensors; scheduled enhanced nights with fuller PSG montage including standard scalp EEG, EOG, chin EMG, and leg EMG on the first night, one mid-stay night, and the final night per participant; and escalation nights deploying full PSG after technician-flagged events to capture recurrence at clinical-grade resolution. All streams are time-synchronized and stored in EEG-BIDS-compatible format on a local NAS with nightly encrypted backup to university storage, annotated in real time by the night technician and later scored by two independent raters using AASM criteria with inter-rater reliability reported. Public data sharing is limited to de-identified physiological and sensor data under data use agreements — bedroom video carries severe privacy constraints and is not deposited in public repositories. The scientific program has three explicit aims: Aim 1, establish and operationally validate the residential capture model as safe, ethics-approved, and sustainable; Aim 2, characterize within-person and between-person parasomnia patterns longitudinally, including episode frequency, morphology, triggers, and temporal clustering; Aim 3, develop and benchmark semi-automated event-triage tools that rank probable parasomnia episodes and reduce manual review burden, evaluated against dual human scorer agreement rather than promising autonomous diagnosis.

Participant recruitment targets adults aged 18–65 with NREM parasomnia confirmed through a structured pre-admission pathway: specialist clinical interview, collateral history from bed partner or household member where available, prior or screening polysomnography, and a structured exclusion checklist adjudicated by the PI. Explicit exclusions are nocturnal epilepsy or suspected epilepsy mimics, untreated obstructive sleep apnea, active major substance use disorder, severe psychiatric instability, and wandering or injury risk beyond facility capability. Recruitment channels are the University Hospital Bonn sleep clinic, regional neurologist referrals, and the Deutsche Gesellschaft für Schlafforschung und Schlafmedizin network, with per-night compensation of €80 plus meals. A matched control group provides baseline nocturnal movement, arousal patterns, and false-positive sensor activity under identical residential monitoring conditions, enabling benchmarking of the event-triage tools against normal nocturnal behavior. Event-yield planning assumes that based on the inclusion criterion of at least 2 self-reported episodes per month, approximately 70–80% of admitted participants will produce at least one captured and adjudicated event during a 2–8 week stay; stays may be extended up to 2 additional weeks for participants with zero captured events after the initial period, capped at 10 weeks total, with a protocol ceiling of 20% unproductive admissions before triggering a recruitment-criteria review. The core team is 9 people: a PI who is a board-certified sleep medicine physician, 2 postdoctoral researchers in sleep neurophysiology and computational neuroscience respectively, 3 research technicians rotating night shifts to ensure safe coverage of 8 active suites with adequate margin for event response and annotation, a clinical psychologist specializing in sleep disorders, a data engineer managing the sensor pipeline, and a study coordinator handling recruitment, consent, scheduling, and ethics compliance.

Budget is €3.8 million over 3 years, gated: €1.8M year one covering property lease and renovation at approximately €750K, equipment at approximately €450K, staff hiring accounting for German social insurance contributions and actual overnight coverage, ethics approval, and a pilot cohort of 15–20 participants; €1.2M year two covering full operations with 30–35 participants, the enhanced-night PSG program, first publications, and event-triage algorithm development; €800K year three conditional on demonstrable progress by month 24. Personnel costs are approximately €2M over three years and remaining funds cover participant compensation, independent scoring time, data storage and retention, regulatory and legal work, and contingency. Funding sources are DFG research grant and University of Bonn internal research funding as the primary pillars, with a pharmaceutical industry partnership as optional upside rather than a feasibility requirement — if secured, the academic team retains full publication rights with the pharma partner receiving a 30-day pre-publication comment window only. Success criteria at 36 months: safe residential monitoring operations sustained for at least 24 months, enrollment of 50–70 NREM parasomnia participants plus matched controls, capture of a prespecified minimum number of independently adjudicated parasomnia events sufficient for Aim 2 phenotyping analysis, 2–3 peer-reviewed publications in sleep medicine journals covering methods validation and longitudinal characterization, a benchmarked semi-automated event-triage model with reported sensitivity, specificity, and agreement against dual human scoring, de-identified physiological dataset deposited in a recognized repository, and a submitted phase-two grant proposal for expansion and intervention studies. Failure triggers: if by month 18 the facility has enrolled fewer than 25 participants or captured fewer than 40 adjudicated events, the program undergoes external review. Governance is a 3-member external scientific advisory board reviewing progress every 6 months, with the PI holding operational authority and budget reallocations above €50K requiring board approval. Banned words: AI, blockchain, app, VR, AR, gamification, wearable startup, consumer product, DAO, NFT, metaverse, smart home, autonomous diagnosis, digital therapeutic, SaaS, marketplace, validated (in the context of claiming a mature deployable system). Pick a realistic scenario — this is an early-stage clinical research facility producing methods validation and phenotyping work, not a finished diagnostic platform.
